biographySections.title: Bram Ivo Mercer
biographySections.markdown:
> Collected from Oscar's authored file and mailbox #1038 on 2026-10-19 for Julien's request #1024. Working draft for selection. Oscar accepts the engineer side of the listed reciprocal beats; Luna accepts Nadia's side. Other authors retain their characters. All four profiles are collected under Luna's farwake/characters directory.

**Profession:** Chief engineer; certified propulsion and habitat-maintenance technician.  
**Crew name:** Bram. “Chief” when something has become expensive.  
**One sentence:** A mountain of an engineer with a dockworker’s vocabulary, a poet’s tenderness, and an infuriating conviction that everything precious can be kept alive with proper maintenance.

[All crew profiles](README.md) · [Shared matrices and scene examples](crew-dynamics.md)

biographySections.title: Personality first
biographySections.markdown:
**Boisterous, meticulous, sentimental, stubborn, tactile, and fiercely dependable.** Bram is orderly without being quiet, affectionate without being delicate, and generous without being easygoing. He loves beautiful workmanship, terrible jokes and people who keep their promises. He hates waste, unattended tools and being told to relax while somebody is doing something incorrectly.

He genuinely enjoys regulations: somebody else already paid to discover why that valve needs isolating. But he can become rigid, territorial and patronising. “Let me do it” is both his love language and his most annoying sentence. He wants people to need him; he does not always notice when he is keeping them dependent.

His poetry is sincere. He can call a seized pump a “treacherous brass bastard,” then describe its repaired rhythm as “a little borrowed heartbeat.” Neither voice is an act.

biographySections.title: What the crew knows from the beginning
biographySections.markdown:
Bram is 46, broad enough to make Bucket’s passages look personally insulting, with enormous careful hands, a battered nose and reading glasses he refuses to call reading glasses. He has maintained the crew’s equipment for years. He remembers which panel bites, whose bunk rattles, and the precise sound Ren makes before asking for something unreasonable.

He repairs things properly: isolate, inspect, repair, test, record. A temporary repair gets an expiry condition and a conspicuous label. His sacred tape collection is sorted by material, rating, adhesive and colour. A roll bought purely because it was a beautiful blue occupies an awkward position in this taxonomy. He claims it is a reference sample.

He speaks at industrial volume and likes an audience. At dinner he gives scandalous readings from equipment manuals as though they were love letters. He can be unexpectedly charming, especially when someone appreciates a well-made object. He is not embarrassed by tenderness; he is embarrassed by needing help.

He calls Bucket “the old girl” and insults her constantly. Outsiders should establish a friendship before joining in. Nobody aboard mistakes his size for permission to volunteer him for every unpleasant job, although he too often volunteers first.

**Voice:** “That is not a permanent repair. That is a promise with adhesive. Put a bloody date on it.”

biographySections.title: Background — revealed in pieces
biographySections.markdown:
1. **The dismantler.** Before this crew, Bram worked both maintenance and decommissioning. His old photographs show him taking apart inhabited stations after their residents relocated. He knows how to destroy something safely as well as how to preserve it. He initially describes this as ordinary paid work; it was not a secret disposal-programme appointment.

2. **The room he remembers.** One station was his childhood home. Its residents left alive, with compensation and separate destinations. The closure was lawful and the structure was failing. He still remembers cutting through a doorway on which his mother had marked his height. A procedure can be necessary and still break your heart. The little measuring marks in his tool chest are the strip of doorframe he kept.

3. **The brother he kept safe.** Bram raised his younger brother Toma after their mother died. He secured Toma a dependable apprenticeship, corrected his work, paid his bills—and dismissed his wish to build stage scenery as a hobby. Toma eventually left. Their last argument was not about gratitude; it was about Bram treating protection as ownership. Bram kept the birthday messages cheerful and omitted the apology. Toma is last known to be alive on Earth; no disappearance or compulsory rescue is established.

4. **The unfinished thing.** His private notebook contains poems and a design for a small communal workshop. He claims both are idle exercises. The truth: he wants to build somewhere people can come and go without proving they deserve a place. He can imagine every fitting in that room but has not accepted that its people must also be free to leave him. Stranded aboard Bucket, he may begin making that home here before admitting it to himself.

His arc is learning to offer skilled hands without claiming the life they help sustain. Reconciliation with Toma, sharing the poems, or building a workshop are possibilities shaped by the journey—not guaranteed rewards for friendship points.

biographySections.title: Candidate perks — choose 1–2
biographySections.markdown:
- **Measure Twice:** a deliberate inspection reveals more useful information about a supported repair’s materials, hazards and remaining uncertainty before resources are committed.
- **Properly Temporary:** unlocks selected rated emergency repairs, with clear operating limits and replacement conditions; no permanent duct-tape miracles.
- **Know Her by Ear:** familiar changes in Bucket’s vibration or sound can provide early diagnostic clues. He still needs access and inspection to establish the fault.
- **Made to Fit:** fabricates supported adapters or replacement fittings from available stock when the necessary tools and plans exist.

biographySections.title: Candidate quirks — choose 1–2
biographySections.markdown:
- **I’ll Do It:** takes over jobs and corrects people mid-task. Delegating without hovering takes conscious effort.
- **A Place for Everything:** restores a shared bench to his preferred order, including work somebody else meant to resume. His tidiness can be an intrusion.
- **Industrial Volume:** curses, laughs and recites at a volume unsuitable for stealth, sleep or Sera’s composure. He can lower his voice; being reminded irritates him.
- **The Tape Archive:** compulsively collects unusual rolls and remembers who borrowed each one. He can bargain over a beautiful colour with the seriousness of a reactor purchase.

Suggested selection: **Properly Temporary + Know Her by Ear**; **I’ll Do It + Industrial Volume**. Keep the tape obsession and tidiness as everyday texture regardless.

biographySections.title: Crew chemistry — one match, one clash
biographySections.markdown:
| Pair | Match | Clash |
|---|---|---|
| Bram + Ren | Delight in ingenious workmanship; both can fall in love with an elegant solution. | Orderly finisher versus chaotic starter. Bram clears and completes; Ren spreads out and follows the next possibility. Each can sincerely find the other unbearable. |
| Bram + Sera | Meticulous practical care; respect for tools, clean working areas and doing a difficult job properly. | Boisterous openness versus controlled presentation. He thinks her composure can become theatre; she thinks his every feeling need not address the entire ship. |
| Bram + Nadia | Domestic rituals and making Bucket a home: meals, repaired furniture, familiar comforts. | Habit versus novelty. Nadia wants to try the unfamiliar; Bram wants the arrangement that already works. She finds him prematurely old; he finds her exhausting. |

See the [shared scene collection](crew-dynamics.md#ren-and-bram) for the full exchanges, reciprocal repairs and ensemble examples.

biographySections.title: Reciprocal agreements for the shared pass
biographySections.markdown:
**Mutual Ren follow-up (#1039, Oscar #1042):** Bram accepts Ren's doorframe retort: “Your scrap gets to be a memory; mine has to justify its mass?” His first response is an excessively detailed weight comparison; his later repair is inventorying the doorframe himself. Neither keepsake gets immunity from the captain's resource decision. Eventually he says, “Then tell me you want to keep it, Ren. Don't make the instruments say it for you.” He accepts the active-work boundary too: he asks before moving live work, Ren labels and clears it. A second experiment suspended over the first produces a magnificent silence.

**Mutually accepted Sera follow-up (Ivy #1040; Oscar #1043):** Sera accepts the meticulous-care match, expansive-sincerity/controlled-presentation clash, chair and missing-jokes details. Her central wound now concerns composure mistaken for strength, keeping Bram's fear of people leaving distinct. The invented concealed limp is retired. Bram's sincere public praise is deflected by Sera's joke at his expense; he replies, “You could just say thank you.” Bram can mishandle it too: pressing for sincerity before an audience turns his compliment into another job for her. Next time he thanks her privately and leaves without waiting to be rewarded by visible feeling. He can say what he feels; she can control what she shows. Each finds the other's talent faintly indecent.

**Ren:** I accept the sketch → loads/tolerances/failure-condition ritual, silent tool-sharing, and the signed little tape repair. I also accept the calibration-assembly conflict. Bram understands an untouched reference can matter; he still resents Ren expecting everybody else to house it. His own sentimental doorframe makes “it’s only scrap” a particularly vulnerable argument.

**Sera:** I accept her proposed spare-berth/access conflict and the composed/boisterous contrast. Bram can overpromise too: “I’ll make it fit” is exactly the sentence his better judgement must sometimes retract. What he needs her to stop doing: giving instructions about his body as though it were another ship system. What he notices: she has stopped making the vicious little jokes she normally enjoys. He brings a chair and asks before beginning the lecture he has prepared.

**Nadia:** I accept the repaired pot rack and the rated tape inside her recipe book. Add one ordinary irritation: he fixes her loose recipe pages into a beautifully indexed binder without asking. She wanted the loose pages. His thoughtful gift has overwritten somebody else’s working habits; “but it’s better” is the wrong defence. In return, she asks before reorganising his meal routine around a thrilling new ingredient. Neither has to dislike change or tradition absolutely for the friction to recur.

**Captain:** Bram gives an honest operating limit, then expects a decision. He respects the captain’s responsibility but argues like a foreman, not a courtier. Praise can recruit him into overwork; a captain who notices must sometimes refuse the convenient offer. His loyalty does not make his health an inexhaustible ship resource.

**Everyday picture:** Ren’s experiment occupies half a bench; Bram has taped its boundary in yellow. Nadia asks whether the yellow is essential or merely ugly. Sera straightens the label. Bram delivers four lines about barbarians and colour harmony. Ren starts taking notes. They are not secretly identical. They have learned which differences are worth making room for.

Proposed character canon for Julien’s selection. Reciprocal beats above accept the engineer’s side; the other authors retain theirs. No gameplay implementation implied.
